Jogae Gui Grilled Clams

Jogae gui is the plainest shellfish record and the one every grill bar runs all summer: a mesh of clams on the grate, a bowl of dipping sauce, and the shells opening on their own schedule — each one pulled the moment it…

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Chapter 02 / 15 seafood recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant — the grill-bar basics, perfected. Jogae gui is the plainest shellfish record and the one every grill bar runs all summer: a mesh of clams on the grate, a bowl of dipping sauce, and the shells opening on their own schedule — each one pulled the moment it gapes and eaten hot with the dip. No butter, no build: the clam's own liquor and the salt-soy dip are the entire dish. The technique is the purge before and the eye at the fire after.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The purge is the recipe's first half: clams spend 30 minutes in cold salted water in a single loose layer, breathing out their sand, then are lifted (not poured — the sand sits in the bottom) and scrubbed. Skip it and every fifth bite is grit; the record's most common failure happens before the fire.
  • Mix the dip and set the table: the clams' pace at the fire leaves no hands free.
  • Fire moderate, grate oiled, or a grill basket that lets the shells sit level; a foil tray with a few knife slits works on a gas grill.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Clams onto the moderate grate in a single layer, hollow-side up where the shells allow. Nothing happens for 2–3 minutes — then they begin to pop open one by one, unevenly, each on its own clock. Checkpoint — an opened clam shows the meat just firmed at the edges and its liquor steaming — that one comes off now, not when its neighbors open. The grill boss works by eye, tongs ready, pulling gapers continuously.
  2. 02
    The discard law at the fire: a clam that stays fully shut after its batch-mates have opened (a full 2-minute grace) does not get forced or knifed — it goes to the discard bowl. Same law as the mussels (#SF13) and oysters (#SF12): the unopened shell is the sea's own warning label. Checkpoint — a test clam with the dip: snap-tender meat, briny liquor, the dip's soy-vinegar line behind it. If the meat is mushy (not springy), that clam was past its day — one is possible in any batch, a pattern means the batch was.
  3. 03
    The pace is the meal: pull, dip, eat, repeat — the platter refills from the grate in waves of five or six, and the last clams off (the stubborn ones) are often the sweetest. Checkpoint — the finish: shells in the bowl, dip nearly gone, and the clam liquor that dripped on the grate has caramelized into a smell the whole table notices — the traditional end at the grill bar is a handful of noodles or rice onto that spot to catch it. Do it; it is the record's secret last course. Chef’s Note — on mixed clams and mixed clocks: manila clams open fast, littlenecks a beat later, and any single species batch still opens unevenly — the record's rhythm is built on that unevenness, pulling each shell in its own moment rather than harvesting a wave. This is the same discipline as the tabletop records' flip-when-it-weeps law (#M01's register): the ingredient announces itself, and the cook's only job is to be watching when it does.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Grit in every biteNo purge or poured from the sand30-minute salt soak; lift, never pour
Clams rubberyPulled late and reheatedOff the fire at first gape, eaten hot
Many stayed shutOld batch or wrong species handlingThe 2-minute grace, then discard; buy tighter shells next time
Dip overwhelms the clamOver-seasoned dipThe dip is a line, not a pool — dunk the meat's edge

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Live clams keep 2 days in an open bowl in the fridge with a damp cloth over them. Cooked, 1 day, meats picked for pasta or jjigae. The dip keeps 3 days.
  • Variations: the butter-gochujang build from the oyster record (#SF12) on the larger clam shells; the mussel pot (#SF13) is the same clams' steamed cousin; the grill's caramelize-and-noodle finish (Method step 3) is the tradition's own variation on itself.
